```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.2,
  out.width = "100%"
)
set.seed(2026)
library(neurothresh)
```

Voxelwise inference is hostile to small focal effects: each voxel pays its
own multiple-testing cost, and a true 2-voxel blob can sit just under the
voxelwise threshold even when its neighbours quietly agree with it. Cluster
and TFCE methods recover that signal by pooling over space, but they pool the
same way everywhere, smoothing local detail away. **LISA** keeps the
locality. It runs the same edge-preserving bilateral filter on the observed
statistic map *and on every matched null draw*, then estimates voxelwise FDR
in the filtered-statistic space. Voxels that align with a coherent local
neighbourhood get amplified; isolated noise spikes get attenuated; the FDR
target is honoured because the null is filtered the same way.

This vignette teaches the full LISA pipeline on a tiny synthetic example you
can step through in seconds.

## First win

Start with a 3D volume that has a small planted blob. Build a null spec from
permuted maps, build a filter, call `lisa()` — the q-value map and rejection
mask come back in a single `neurothresh_result`.

```{r quick-data, include = FALSE}
dims <- c(10L, 10L, 10L)
make_smooth <- function() {
  raw <- array(rnorm(prod(dims)), dims)
  out <- raw
  for (i in 2:(dims[1] - 1)) for (j in 2:(dims[2] - 1)) for (k in 2:(dims[3] - 1)) {
    out[i, j, k] <- mean(raw[(i - 1):(i + 1), (j - 1):(j + 1), (k - 1):(k + 1)])
  }
  out * sqrt(27)
}
plant_blob <- function(z, amp = 10) {
  z[4:7, 4:7, 4:7] <- z[4:7, 4:7, 4:7] + amp
  z
}
z <- plant_blob(make_smooth(), amp = 10)
nulls <- replicate(60, make_smooth(), simplify = FALSE)
```

```{r quick-pipeline}
ns <- null_from_maps(z, nulls)
filt <- lisa_bilateral(radius = 1, n_iter = 1)
fit <- lisa(stat_vol = ns$stat_vol, mask = ns$mask, null_spec = ns,
            filter = filt,
            tail = "pos", q = 0.10)
fit
```

```{r quick-checks, include = FALSE}
truth <- array(FALSE, dims)
truth[4:7, 4:7, 4:7] <- TRUE
reject <- as.logical(fit$reject)
stopifnot(inherits(fit, "neurothresh_result"))
stopifnot(identical(fit$method, "lisa"))
stopifnot(sum(reject) > 0)
stopifnot(sum(reject) < prod(dims) / 5)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.numeric(fit$pvals))))
stopifnot(any(reject & as.vector(truth)))
```

```{r quick-fig, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "Mid-axial slice of the planted-blob example: input Z, filtered statistic, q-value map, and the LISA rejection mask."}
slice_at <- ceiling(dims[3] / 2)
slice_matrix <- function(x, z = slice_at) {
  matrix(as.numeric(x)[((z - 1) * prod(dims[1:2]) + 1):(z * prod(dims[1:2]))],
         nrow = dims[1])
}
img <- function(m, main, zlim = NULL, col = hcl.colors(80, "Viridis")) {
  if (is.null(zlim)) zlim <- range(m, na.rm = TRUE, finite = TRUE)
  image(seq_len(nrow(m)), seq_len(ncol(m)), m,
        zlim = zlim, col = col, main = main,
        xlab = "", ylab = "", axes = FALSE, asp = 1)
}
truth_slice <- slice_matrix(truth)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
img(slice_matrix(z), main = "Input Z")
contour(seq_len(dims[1]), seq_len(dims[2]), truth_slice, levels = 0.5,
        add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "white", lwd = 2)
filtered <- as.numeric(lisa_filtered_stat(fit))
img(slice_matrix(array(filtered, dim = dims)), main = "Filtered statistic")
contour(seq_len(dims[1]), seq_len(dims[2]), truth_slice, levels = 0.5,
        add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "white", lwd = 2)
q_slice <- slice_matrix(fit$pvals)
img(q_slice, main = "q-values", zlim = c(0, 1), col = hcl.colors(64, "Inferno"))
contour(seq_len(dims[1]), seq_len(dims[2]), truth_slice, levels = 0.5,
        add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "white", lwd = 2)
rej <- slice_matrix(fit$reject)
img(rej, main = "Reject mask", zlim = c(0, 1),
    col = c("grey90", "firebrick"))
contour(seq_len(dims[1]), seq_len(dims[2]), truth_slice, levels = 0.5,
        add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "black", lwd = 2)
par(op)
```

The blob lights up in the filtered map (smoother peak), survives at q ≤ 0.10,
and the rejection mask localises it without bleeding far outside its true
support.

## The mental model

LISA has four objects you compose:

| Object | Built by | Role |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `neurothresh_null_spec` | `null_from_maps()`, `null_one_sample()`, `null_two_sample()`, `null_glm()`, ... | Bundles the observed map, mask, and a deterministic-by-index draw function |
| `neurothresh_lisa_filter` | `lisa_bilateral()` | Specifies radius, range/space sigmas, and iterations |
| inference call | `lisa(stat_vol, mask, null_spec, filter, ...)` | Filters the observed map and every null draw, then runs FDR in filtered space |
| `neurothresh_result` | returned by `lisa()` | Method-tagged object with `pvals` (q-values), `reject`, and `extras$filtered_stat` |

The pipeline is always the same shape: **build inputs → build a null spec →
build a filter → call `lisa()` → inspect the result.** The wrappers
`lisa_onesample()`, `lisa_twosample()`, and `lisa_glm()` chain steps 1–3 for
common designs.

## Tuning the bilateral filter

The filter has two scales:

- `sigma_space` controls how far in **physical neighbourhood** the filter
  averages — bigger σ pools across more voxels.
- `sigma_range` controls how much **statistic disagreement** is tolerated —
  bigger σ pools across more value differences (less edge-preserving).

`radius` caps the neighbourhood at ±r voxels. `n_iter > 1` re-applies the
filter, sharpening edges. LISA uses `neuroim2::bilateral_filter()`, whose
neighborhoods are mask-normalized by default, so edge voxels are not dragged
toward out-of-mask or out-of-bounds zeros.

```{r filter-sweep, fig.cap = "Three filter settings on the same observed map: tight, default, and loose. Each panel shows the same axial slice after one iteration."}
filters <- list(
  tight   = lisa_bilateral(radius = 1, sigma_space = 0.7, sigma_range = 1,
                            n_iter = 1),
  default = lisa_bilateral(radius = 1, n_iter = 1),
  loose   = lisa_bilateral(radius = 1, sigma_space = 1.5, sigma_range = 4,
                            n_iter = 1)
)
filtered <- lapply(filters, function(f) {
  fit_f <- lisa(stat_vol = ns$stat_vol, mask = ns$mask, null_spec = ns,
                filter = f, tail = "pos", q = 0.10)
  as.numeric(lisa_filtered_stat(fit_f))
})
```

```{r filter-sweep-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(length(filtered) == length(filters))
stopifnot(all(vapply(filtered, function(x) all(is.finite(x)), logical(1))))
```

```{r filter-sweep-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.7}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
zlim <- range(unlist(filtered), finite = TRUE)
for (nm in names(filtered)) {
  s <- matrix(filtered[[nm]][((slice_at - 1) * prod(dims[1:2]) + 1):
                              (slice_at * prod(dims[1:2]))],
              nrow = dims[1])
  image(seq_len(nrow(s)), seq_len(ncol(s)), s,
        col = hcl.colors(80, "Viridis"), zlim = zlim,
        main = nm, xlab = "", ylab = "", axes = FALSE, asp = 1)
  contour(seq_len(dims[1]), seq_len(dims[2]), truth_slice, levels = 0.5,
          add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "white", lwd = 2)
}
par(op)
```

A **tight** filter behaves close to voxelwise inference: it preserves edges
but pools little. A **loose** filter behaves more like cluster inference:
the blob spreads into a soft halo. The default sits between them. You usually
want defaults; reach for tighter settings when peaks are dense and edges
matter, looser settings when effects are diffuse.

## From subject maps

When you have subject-level images, the `lisa_onesample()` wrapper builds the
null spec for you using `null_one_sample()`. The same `tail`, `q`, `filter`,
and storage arguments flow through.

```{r onesample}
imgs <- replicate(8, plant_blob(make_smooth(), amp = 2.5), simplify = FALSE)
one <- lisa_onesample(
  imgs,
  n_perm = 24,
  seed = 1,
  filter = lisa_bilateral(radius = 1, n_iter = 1),
  tail = "pos",
  q = 0.20
)
one
```

```{r onesample-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(inherits(one, "neurothresh_result"))
stopifnot(identical(one$method, "lisa"))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.numeric(one$pvals))))
```

Two-group designs use `lisa_twosample(imgs, group, ...)`. Anything more
involved — covariates, nuisance regressors, between-subject contrasts — uses
`lisa_glm(imgs, design, contrast, ...)` and is the recommended path whenever
the analysis is not strictly one- or two-sample.

## External statistic maps

Use `null_from_maps()` when the observed map and the permuted null maps come
from a different pipeline (an MVPA searchlight, a cluster job, a permutation
saved to disk):

```{r external}
ns_ext <- null_from_maps(z, nulls)
fit_ext <- lisa(stat_vol = ns_ext$stat_vol, mask = ns_ext$mask,
                null_spec = ns_ext,
                filter = lisa_bilateral(radius = 1, n_iter = 1), tail = "pos", q = 0.10)
sum(fit_ext$reject)
```

```{r external-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(inherits(fit_ext, "neurothresh_result"))
stopifnot(identical(dim(fit_ext$reject), dims))
```

The list of permuted maps must use the same observed-map dimensions; LISA
does not re-mask or re-canonicalise external inputs.

## A null spec is reusable

The same `null_spec` can drive both LISA and other neurothresh inference
methods, so you can compare local-adaptive FDR against, e.g., scale-space
localised energy without re-permuting:

```{r shared-null}
sse <- scale_space_energy(
  null_spec = ns,
  scales = scale_space(2, include_global = FALSE),
  statistics = list(signed_coherence(tail = "two")),
  n_perm = ns$n_perm
)
summary(sse)
```

```{r shared-null-checks, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(inherits(sse, "scale_space_energy_result"))
stopifnot(is.data.frame(summary(sse)))
```

This is the canonical neurothresh contract in action: build the null once,
spend it across whichever inference methods answer your scientific question.

## Inspecting the result

`fit` is a standard `neurothresh_result`, so the same accessors work as for
every other inference method in the package. The LISA-specific bits live
under `extras`:

```{r inspect}
fit$threshold
sum(fit$reject)
range(as.numeric(fit$pvals), finite = TRUE)
lambda <- lisa_filtered_stat(fit)
range(as.numeric(lambda), finite = TRUE)
names(fit$extras)
```

`fit$pvals` is the voxelwise q-value volume, monotone in evidence by default.
`fit$reject` is the rejection mask at the supplied `q`. `extras$filtered_stat`
is the filtered observed map (the same shape as `stat_vol`); use
`lisa_filtered_stat(fit)` rather than reaching into `extras` directly.

For diagnostics — sanity-checking the filter, plotting the filtered null
distribution at a voxel — pass `store_filtered_nulls = TRUE`. Only do this on
small runs; the full filtered-null matrix is `n_perm × sum(mask)`.

## Implementation note

LISA has one filtering implementation: `neuroim2::bilateral_filter()` from
neuroim2 0.16.0 or later. Its neighborhoods are mask-normalized by default.
When `filter$scale = "sd_first_30_nulls"`, the range scale is estimated from
early null maps and passed as `range_scale`, so the observed map and every null
draw use the same intensity bandwidth. This is the synchronized filtering
contract needed for LISA-style inference.

Filter weights depend on each statistic map (the bilateral kernel uses the
voxel values themselves), so there is no shared weight matrix to amortise
across draws. The cost of LISA is dominated by `n_perm` filter applications;
plan accordingly.
